target: Hallo, mag ik binnenkomen?
english: Hello, may I come in?
old: Modal verb sits second; the main verb jumps to the end. Ik moet morgen vroeg opstaan (I have to get up early tomorrow). Brackets the sentence.
focus: Modal-bracket IS true here: quote this card's own 'mag ik binnenkomen' – modal 'mag' second, main verb 'binnenkomen' to the end. Drop the unrelated moeten example.

target: Hallo, ik kom je ophalen.
english: Hello, I'm coming to pick you up.
old: Dutch has two 'you's: `je/jij` (informal – friends, family, peers) and `u` (formal – strangers, elders, business). They use different verb forms: `jij hebt` vs `u hebt` (or `u heeft`).
focus: Introduce informal vs formal 'you': anchor this card's 'je' (informal) and contrast with 'u' (strangers/elders). Strip backticks, one rule, no verb-form table.

target: Prettig kennis met u te maken.
english: Pleased to make your acquaintance.
old: `Je` (unstressed) vs `jij` (stressed/contrastive) – same word, just emphasis. Possessive: `je/jouw boek` (your book, informal) vs `uw boek` (formal).
focus: This card actually uses formal 'u' ('kennis met u te maken') – rewrite to explain u = the polite you for strangers/formal settings, quoting 'u'. Strip backticks.

target: Doei, ik zie je morgen weer!
english: Bye, I'll see you again tomorrow!
old: Modern Dutch trends toward `je` even with strangers. But in customer service, with older people, or in writing – default to `u`.
focus: Keep the usage nuance (modern Dutch drifts to 'je', but default to 'u' in service/writing/with elders), anchor the card's 'je'. Strip backticks, tighten.

target: Ik geloof dat hij gelijk heeft.
english: I believe that he is right.
old: Subordinating conjunctions (`dat`, `omdat`, `als`, `terwijl`, `nadat`) send the verb to the end of the clause: `Ik weet dat hij komt`.
focus: Verb-final is true here: quote 'dat hij gelijk heeft' – 'dat' pushes the verb 'heeft' to the end. Strip backticks, drop the extra generic example.

target: Zij heeft geen broers of zussen.
english: She has no brothers or sisters.
old: `geen` negates a noun without article: `ik heb geen geld` (I have no money). `Niet` negates everything else: `ik kom niet` (I'm not coming).
focus: geen/niet split IS live here: anchor 'geen broers of zussen' (geen negates the article-less noun) vs niet for everything else. Strip backticks.

target: Mijn schoonmoeder komt vanavond eten.
english: My mother-in-law is coming for dinner tonight.
old: "Schoonmoeder" – 'schoon' in family terms means 'in-law'.
focus: Frame the productive pattern, not the single word: 'schoon-' prefixes family terms to mean in-law (schoonmoeder, schoonvader, schoonzus), quoting schoonmoeder.

target: Gisteren kocht zij een nieuwe fiets.
english: Yesterday she bought a new bicycle.
old: Dutch follows V2 like German: the verb stays in second position. `Vandaag ga ik` (today I go), not `vandaag ik ga`. Subject jumps after the verb when something else opens the sentence.
focus: This card is a perfect V2 demo: quote 'Gisteren kocht zij' – time-word first forces verb 'kocht' second, subject 'zij' after. Strip backticks, drop the vandaag example.

target: Dag schat, ik heb je gemist vandaag.
english: Hi darling, I missed you today.
old: Perfect = `hebben/zijn` + past participle. Most verbs use `hebben`: `ik heb gegeten`, `wij hebben gezien`. Participle to the end of the sentence.
focus: Perfect structure is live here: quote 'ik heb je gemist' – hebben + participle 'gemist' lands at the end. Strip backticks, drop the generic examples.

target: Tot straks, ik ga even boodschappen doen.
english: See you later, I'm going grocery shopping.
old: 'Gaan' (to go) is irregular: 'ik ga', 'jij gaat'. Used to express near future.
focus: Keep only the useful half: gaan + infinitive = near future (like English 'going to'), anchor 'ik ga ... doen'. Drop the gaan conjugation table.

target: Ik stap over op een andere lijn bij station Sloterdijk.
english: I transfer to another line at station Sloterdijk.
old: 'Overstappen' = to transfer – essential Dutch transit verb.
focus: Drop the vocab gloss; the card demonstrates a separable verb – overstappen splits so the prefix moves ('ik stap over ... op'). Explain the split, anchor 'stap over'.

target: Ik ben geboren in België.
english: I was born in Belgium.
old: Perfect tense with `zijn` for movement/change verbs: `ik ben gegaan` (I went), `hij is gestorven` (he died). Same split as French/Italian/German.
focus: Anchor on 'ik ben geboren' – Dutch uses zijn (not hebben) in the perfect for change-of-state verbs like geboren; strip backticks and the French/Italian/German aside.

target: Ik heb geen idee waar hij is.
english: I have no idea where he is.
old: If you'd say 'no X' in English, use `geen X` in Dutch. If you'd say 'not X' (verb / adjective / adverb), use `niet`.
focus: geen vs niet, anchored on 'geen idee'; strip backticks, keep the no-X/not-X test in plain text.

target: Er staan vijfduizend bomen in dit stadspark.
english: There are five thousand trees in this city park.
old: `er` has many uses; the most common is existential: `er is`, `er zijn` = 'there is / there are'. Don't try to translate `er` literally – it's just a filler subject.
focus: Existential er anchored on 'Er staan ... bomen' – er is a dummy subject for 'there is/are', don't translate it; strip backticks, one rule.

target: Zij heeft een appeltje te schillen met haar collega.
english: She has a bone to pick with her colleague.
old: 'Een appeltje te schillen hebben' = to have a bone to pick.
focus: Give the literal image: 'een appeltje te schillen' = a little apple to peel = a bone to pick; don't just re-echo the English idiom the translation already shows.

target: Kun je morgen een uurtje eerder op kantoor zijn?
english: Can you be at the office an hour earlier tomorrow?
old: Dutch has two 'you's: `je/jij` (informal – friends, family, peers) and `u` (formal – strangers, elders, business). They use different verb forms: `jij hebt` vs `u hebt` (or `u heeft`).
focus: The core je vs u distinction anchored on 'Kun je'; strip backticks, one rule (informal je/jij vs formal u), drop the paradigm list.

target: Gelukkig kwam de bus precies op tijd.
english: Fortunately the bus came exactly on time.
old: V2: adverb 'gelukkig' in position 1, verb 'kwam' immediately follows.
focus: Verb-second trap: after a fronted word Dutch flips verb before subject. Quote 'Gelukkig kwam de bus', drop the 'V2:' jargon, contrast with English order.

target: Spreekt u Engels?
english: Do you speak English?
old: Yes/no questions just swap subject and verb – no 'do' helper like English.
focus: Keep the no-'do'-helper contrast; anchor it by quoting the card's 'Spreekt u Engels?'.

target: Na de les gaan de studenten naar huis.
english: After the class the students go home.
old: V2 rule: the finite verb is always the second element in main clauses.
focus: Anchor V2 to this card: fronting 'Na de les' forces the verb 'gaan' ahead of subject 'de studenten' (verb stays second).

target: De kinderen zijn naar het strand gerend.
english: The children ran to the beach.
old: Perfectum with 'zijn': 'rennen' (movement) → 'zijn gerend'.
focus: Motion-to-a-destination takes 'zijn' not 'hebben' where English always uses 'have': 'zijn ... gerend'.

target: Hij hoeft het rapport niet vandaag af te hebben.
english: He doesn't have to finish the report today.
old: Modal verbs push the main verb to the end as infinitive: 'ik moet werken'.
focus: Modal/hoeven sends the main verb to the clause end; quote this card's tail 'niet vandaag af te hebben'.

target: Er is geen melk meer in de koelkast voor het ontbijt morgenochtend.
english: There is no milk left in the fridge for breakfast tomorrow morning.
old: `er` has many uses; the most common is existential: `er is`, `er zijn` = 'there is / there are'. Don't try to translate `er` literally – it's just a filler subject.
focus: Strip backticks; anchor to 'Er is geen melk' — 'er' is a dummy subject in there-is/there-are, don't translate it literally. Keep to one rule.

target: Hij is groter dan zijn oudere broer.
english: He is taller than his older brother.
old: Comparison: adjective + -er + 'dan' = than. 'Groot' → 'groter'.
focus: Card has 'groter dan' – the real trap is 'dan' = than; Dutch learners often wrongly say 'groter als'. Standard is 'groter dan'. Skip the -er paradigm (parallels English).

target: Doordat zij te laat vertrok, miste zij de trein.
english: Because she left too late, she missed the train.
old: 'Doordat' = because (cause-effect) – verb-final.
focus: 'doordat' = because as a direct cause/result (often unintended), vs 'omdat' (reason/motive); verb goes to clause end (vertrok). Quote 'Doordat zij te laat vertrok'. Drop the 'verb-final' jargon.

target: Hij is de gebeten hond na het slechte nieuws.
english: He became the scapegoat after the bad news.
old: 'De gebeten hond zijn' = to be the scapegoat.
focus: Reveal the literal image: 'de gebeten hond' = literally 'the bitten dog' – the one everyone blames/takes the fall. Don't just re-translate to 'scapegoat'.

target: Hoe langer de fietsenstalling leeg blijft staan, hoe meer klachten de gemeente ontvangt.
english: The longer the bicycle parking stays empty, the more complaints the municipality receives.
old: 'Hoe...hoe' double comparative + compound 'fietsenstalling' + 'gemeente'.
focus: 'hoe + comparative ... hoe + comparative' = English 'the more... the more'. Quote 'hoe langer... hoe meer'. Drop the compound-noun laundry list.

target: Behalve op vrijdag heeft het museum elke dag open.
english: The museum is open every day except Friday.
old: 'Behalve' exception phrase in P1 – triggers inversion.
focus: Fronting an element (Behalve op vrijdag) forces the verb second, so subject follows: 'heeft het museum'. Plain words – no 'P1'/'inversion' jargon.

target: Zij vraagt of wij mee willen gaan naar het feest.
english: She asks if we want to come along to the party.
old: Subordinate with 'of': verb-final – 'willen gaan' at the end.
focus: 'of' here = whether/if; it sends the verb cluster to the clause end: 'willen gaan'. Quote the card. Lead with the surprise, not 'Subordinate with of'.

target: De bestelling wordt morgen door de koerier bezorgd.
english: The order will be delivered tomorrow by the courier.
old: Passive with 'worden' + past participle for actions in progress.
focus: 'worden' + participle = the passive: 'wordt... bezorgd' = is being delivered; 'door' marks the doer (door de koerier = by the courier). Quote the card, drop 'past participle' jargon.

target: Als het mooi weer is, gaan wij naar het strand.
english: If the weather is nice, we go to the beach.
old: 'Als' = if/when – verb-final in the als-clause, V2 in main clause.
focus: In the als-clause the verb goes last ('is'), but the main clause keeps the verb second ('gaan'): 'Als het mooi weer is, gaan wij...'. Spell it out, no 'V2'.

target: Zet de muziek wat zachter, de buren klagen al over het lawaai.
english: Turn the music down a bit, the neighbors are already complaining about the noise.
old: Dutch imperative = verb stem: 'Kom!' (Come!). Add 'u' for formal: 'Komt u binnen!' For 'we': 'Laten we gaan!' (Let's go!).
focus: Anchor on the card's own imperative 'Zet' (bare stem). Add the formal 'u' and 'laten we' collective forms tersely. Drop the all-generic Kom!/Komt u examples that don't cite the card.

target: Wij gaan niet naar buiten omdat het hard regent.
english: We don't go outside because it is raining hard.
old: Tricky: `omdat` (because) sends the verb to the end of the clause; `want` (because) does not – same English translation, different word-order rules.
focus: Strip the backticks. 'omdat' and 'want' both = because, but 'omdat' sends the verb to the clause end (regent) while 'want' keeps normal order. Quote 'omdat het hard regent'.

target: De brief is gisteren verstuurd en zal morgen waarschijnlijk worden bezorgd.
english: The letter was sent yesterday and will probably be delivered tomorrow.
old: Dutch passive uses 'worden' (action) or 'zijn' (state): 'Het huis wordt gebouwd' vs 'Het huis is gebouwd'. 'Er' often starts impersonal passives.
focus: Contrast worden (future action: 'zal worden bezorgd') vs zijn (state: 'is verstuurd') — this card shows both; quote them and cut the tacked-on 'Er' aside (one rule).

target: Ik zou graag meer willen weten over de geschiedenis van dit oude gebouw.
english: I would like to know more about the history of this old building.
old: Polite alternative to `willen`: `Ik zou graag…` (I would like…) for soft requests. `Ik wil` can sound abrupt; `Ik zou graag` is the polite form.
focus: Politeness: 'Ik wil' can sound blunt; 'Ik zou graag ... willen' softens a request. Strip the backticks, quote 'Ik zou graag', keep it one clause.

target: Er worden veel fietsen gestolen in de grote steden.
english: Many bicycles are stolen in the big cities.
old: 'Er' + passive: impersonal passive – no specific subject.
focus: Dutch opens a subjectless passive with 'er': 'er worden veel fietsen gestolen' = bikes get stolen, no named agent. Drop the 'impersonal passive' jargon lead.

target: Ik heb er vijf nodig voor het recept.
english: I need five of them for the recipe.
old: Partitive 'er': 'er vijf' = five of them.
focus: A bare number needs 'er' meaning 'of them': 'ik heb er vijf nodig' = I need five of them. Lead with the trap, not the word 'partitive'.

target: Ik denk er vaak aan hoe het vroeger was.
english: I often think about how it used to be.
old: Prepositional 'er': 'eraan' = er + aan – think about it.
focus: Prepositional 'er' splits from its preposition when a word intervenes: 'ik denk er vaak aan' = I often think about it (er ... aan wrapping 'vaak'). Dutch can't say 'aan het' for things.

target: Hoi, zullen we samen gaan?
english: Hi, shall we go together?
old: 'Zullen' + infinitive forms the future: 'ik zal gaan' (I will go). Often replaced by present tense + time word.
focus: In a question 'zullen we...?' = 'shall we...?', a suggestion — zullen is not only the future auxiliary. Quote 'zullen we samen gaan'; drop the future-tense framing that this card does not use.

target: Ik ben vandaag te moe om nog naar het feest van mijn collega te gaan.
english: I am too tired today to still go to my colleague's party.
old: 'Om te' + infinitive expresses purpose: 'Ik ga naar huis om te slapen'. 'Zonder te' = without: 'Zonder te kijken' (without looking).
focus: 'te + adjective + om ... te' = 'too ... to': 'te moe om ... te gaan' = too tired to go. Quote the card and drop the external examples and the second (zonder te) rule.

target: Lekker weertje vandaag hè?
english: Nice weather today, right?
old: Commenting on weather with 'lekker weertje' is peak Dutch small talk.
focus: Sentence-final 'hè' is a tag = 'right?'/'isn't it?' seeking agreement: 'lekker weertje, hè?'. Chill+factual, cut 'peak Dutch small talk'.

target: Ondanks de vertraging arriveerden wij op tijd.
english: Despite the delay we arrived on time.
old: 'Ondanks' = despite – preposition, not conjunction.
focus: 'ondanks' takes a noun ('ondanks de vertraging'), not a clause; for a clause use 'hoewel' or 'ondanks dat'. Anchor to the card, drop the preposition/conjunction labels.

target: Hij zoekt een rustige plek om te studeren.
english: He looks for a quiet place to study.
old: 'Om te' without specified subject – general purpose.
focus: Purpose wraps the infinitive: 'om ... te' = 'in order to' — 'om te studeren' = to study; om at the front, te just before the infinitive.

target: Desondanks bleef hij optimistisch over de toekomst.
english: Nevertheless he remained optimistic about the future.
old: 'Desondanks' = nevertheless – formal connector, causes inversion.
focus: Plain words, no 'connector/inversion' jargon: front an adverb like desondanks and the verb jumps ahead of the subject – 'Desondanks bleef hij', not 'hij bleef'.

target: Hij vergat de deur op slot te doen.
english: He forgot to lock the door.
old: 'Vergeten te' – without 'om', direct infinitive.
focus: Vergeten takes plain 'te', no 'om': 'de deur op slot te doen'. Contrast the om-te verbs so the learner knows when om drops.

target: Wij zijn begonnen met het opruimen van de zolder.
english: We started cleaning up the attic.
old: 'Beginnen met het' + infinitive-as-noun – alternative to 'om te'.
focus: Drop 'infinitive-as-noun' jargon: Dutch turns a verb into a noun with 'het' – 'het opruimen' = the cleaning-up, so 'beginnen met het opruimen' = start the tidying.

target: Wij kregen te horen dat de vlucht was geannuleerd.
english: We were told that the flight had been cancelled.
old: 'Kregen te horen dat' = were told that.
focus: Surface the literal logic: 'krijgen te horen' = literally 'get to hear' = to be told. Quote 'kregen te horen dat'.
